newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to discuss Irish fish cuts compromise.
newsitem.headline: EU to discuss Irish fish cuts compromise.

text.p: European Union fisheries ministers will discuss on Friday an Irish compromise over proposals to cut fish catches sharply and protect depleted stocks, EU officials said.

Ireland, the current EU president, this week suggested easing fierce cuts proposed by the European Commission, putting emphasis on limiting fishing effort instead of cutting fleets and halving the programme period to three years.
"It's clearly better but needs detailed study," said an official, expressing the view of major fishing member states.
But only Greece, Italy, Germany and Portugal were at all positive when the Irish text was presented to member state fisheries officials in Brussels.
Britain has warned it will not implement any further major cuts until the problem of "quota hoppers" -- boats from one EU state which register in another to take part of its quota -- is resolved.
Around 20 percent of the British national fish quota is now caught by some 150 foreign, mainly Spanish and Dutch, vessels.
Some officials said that the current five-year fishing reduction programme, which expires at the end of December, could be extended for another year.
Ministers will be preoccupied with fixing 1997 fish catch quotas at their meeting in December, they said.
But the European Commission said it will press hard for a framework agreement this year. Detailed reduction plans would then be negotiated with the EU's 13 fishing member states.

"It would be irresponsible not to have a new programme by January 1," Commission fisheries spokesman Filippo di Robilant said. "It would be a very bad sign to the fishing industry. We cannot delay restructuring."
In May, the EU's executive proposed fish catch cuts of up to 40 percent over six years for the most endangered stocks, such as North Sea cod, plaice, sole, herring and mackerel.
Ireland has now suggested a 20 percent cut over three years, compared with a 24 percent cut sought by the Commission.

The Commission is also unhappy that the Irish compromise puts too much emphasis on reducing fishing effort -- time spent fishing specific fish stocks in specific areas -- and controlling fishing gear.
"Permanent measures are needed, that's to say a reduction in fishing capacity," Di Robilant said.
But the EU's executive said it could accept an Irish proposal to raise the size of small coastal vessels exempted from the cuts to 10 metres, from seven.
